title: Neighbouring groups
goal: Spot a nucleophile inside the molecule that reaches a reacting carbon first, and follow the small ring it makes to the product.

problemSets.title: Anchimeric assistance
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A lone pair in the same molecule pushes out the leaving group before any outside nucleophile can.
problemSets.conceptCard:
A nucleophile that is **part of the same molecule** is always close to the reacting carbon, so it can win easily against a nucleophile from the solution. When it displaces the leaving group, the reaction is faster than expected: **anchimeric assistance** (neighbouring group participation).

The signs:

- **a fast reaction** at a carbon that should be slow (a primary chloride, a secondary tosylate)
- **first-order kinetics**: the rate does not depend on the outside nucleophile
- **retention of configuration**: the neighbouring group attacks from behind (inversion), then the outside nucleophile opens the ring (a second inversion)

Good neighbouring groups have lone pairs: **sulfur** and **nitrogen** (three-membered *episulfonium* and *aziridinium* ions), and the **carbonyl oxygen of an ester**, which reaches round to make a five-membered *acetoxonium* ion. The neighbouring group must sit **anti** to the leaving group. The app does not check stereochemistry yet.

setItems.whyThisOne: A reminder: a bromine bridges two carbons, then bromide opens the three-membered ring from behind.
Sulfur pushes out chloride: why mustard gas is so dangerous.
An ester carbonyl oxygen joins in: two inversions give retention.

problemSets.title: Epoxides
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Acid: the nucleophile goes to the more substituted carbon. Base: to the less hindered one.
problemSets.conceptCard:
An epoxide is a three-membered ring, strained by about 110 kJ mol⁻¹, so even an alkoxide can be its leaving group. Which carbon the nucleophile attacks depends on the conditions:

- **basic or neutral** (methoxide, hydroxide, amines): a plain SN2 reaction at the **less hindered** carbon
- **acidic**: the protonated epoxide has its weaker, longer C–O bond to the **more substituted** carbon, which carries most of the positive charge, so a weak nucleophile attacks there

In both cases the nucleophile comes in from the face opposite the oxygen: **inversion**, and *anti* opening on a ring.

An alkoxide next to an epoxide is a neighbouring group too. It opens the epoxide inside the molecule and closes a new one: the **Payne rearrangement**, an equilibrium between two epoxy alcohols.

setItems.whyThisOne: Methoxide picks the less hindered carbon.
The same epoxide in acid: methanol picks the more substituted carbon.
An alkoxide as the neighbouring group: the epoxide walks along the chain.

problemSets.title: Ring contractions
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A carbanion displaces a halide on the next-but-one carbon; the small ring formed then breaks a different way.
problemSets.conceptCard:
A carbanion or enolate can also be the neighbouring group. With a halogen on the carbon on the other side of a C=O or SO₂ group, it closes a **three-membered ring**, which then opens or falls apart in a new direction:

- **Favorskii**: an α-haloketone with an alkoxide. The enolate closes a **cyclopropanone**; the alkoxide adds to it and a ring C–C bond breaks. A cyclic α-chloroketone gives a ring **one carbon smaller**, as an ester
- **Ramberg–Bäcklund**: an α-halo sulfone with hydroxide. The carbanion closes an **episulfone**, which loses **SO₂**, leaving a C=C bond where the sulfone was

In both, look for the acidic hydrogen on the side **away from** the halogen: that is the carbanion that can reach the C–halogen carbon.

setItems.whyThisOne: A six-membered ring ketone becomes a five-membered ring ester.
Close a ring, then lose SO₂: a sulfone becomes an alkene.

problemSets.title: Checkpoint
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Which neighbour attacks, which small ring forms, and how does it open?
problemSets.conceptCard: Reactions from every set, shuffled, names hidden until you finish. Three attempts per step.

setItems.whyThisOne: Which atom pushes out the chloride?
A neighbour with a carbonyl oxygen.
An alkoxide next to an epoxide.
A ketone becomes a smaller-ring ester.
From a sulfone to an alkene.
